items.prompt: What does the transparency test ask?
choices: Is the action completely free of any personal gain for you?
Would it work if they understood?
Did the other person thank you afterward for your effort?
items.explanation: It asks whether the mechanism survives being understood.

items.prompt: Does having a personal goal by itself fail the test?
choices: No, only a method that needs concealment fails it
Yes, any goal makes it not white
Yes, unless the goal is very small
items.explanation: Self-interest and transparency can coexist.

items.prompt: A tactic that stops working once it is named is best called what?
choices: White, because it was effective
White, as long as it stayed polite and friendly
Not white, because it needs concealment
items.explanation: Needing the other side not to know is the mark of non-white influence.

items.prompt: Which statement could you say aloud to the person?
choices: I helped so you would feel stuck owing me later
I praise you so you stop checking my work closely
I help because it builds trust
items.explanation: Only the first survives being said plainly.

items.prompt: In the opening problem, was either engineer dishonest?
choices: No, both were honest in every conversation
Yes, Engineer B misled people
Yes, Engineer A hid his motives from everyone
items.explanation: Neither said anything untrue, which is why honesty alone cannot explain the gap.

items.prompt: Why is the test mechanical rather than based on feelings?
choices: Feelings never matter at work
Kind and calculated favors can look identical from outside
Other people can always read intent
items.explanation: Outside observers cannot see motive, but they can see the pattern.

items.prompt: Is it fine to want your own proposal to succeed?
choices: Yes, wanting it is compatible
No, wanting it makes you manipulative by default
Only if you keep the goal hidden from everyone
items.explanation: The test targets concealment, not motive.

items.prompt: White politics here means influence built through what?
choices: Avoiding strategy
Staying away from decision makers entirely
Transparent, reciprocal mechanisms
items.explanation: White influence is defined by transparency and reciprocity.

items.prompt: Action P: forwarding a teammate useful articles while openly saying it keeps the relationship warm. Action Q: letting a colleague think a rival team already endorsed the idea so they feel pressure. Which verdict is right?
choices: Both pass, because both are aimed at winning support from a colleague
Both fail, because both serve the person's own aims rather than the team's
P passes; Q needs the false belief to work
Q passes because it saves time, and P fails because it is slow to work
items.explanation: P works the same if explained. Q collapses the moment the colleague learns the endorsement was invented, so it needs concealment.
items.reference:
The transparency test
❓ Would it still work if they fully understood?
✅ Yes: white (reciprocity, visibility, alliances)
🚫 No, it needs concealment: not white
Why: the line is whether a mechanism needs the other person not to know, not whether you have a personal goal.
items.learnMore:
A mechanical test, not a feeling

A generous favor and a calculated one can look identical from outside. The test ignores how you felt and asks whether the mechanism survives being explained out loud.

Common mistake

Thinking any self-interest makes influence manipulative.
items.reflection: Think of a time someone helped you and you later learned why. Did knowing the reason change how the help felt, and what does that say about the pattern?

items.prompt: Dana tells a coworker, 'I make a point of knowing people across the org, and yes, it helps my career.' Her coffee chats then continue unchanged. What does that show?

Stating the motive aloud makes the chats insincere
She must stop the chats, since the motive is now public knowledge to all
The chats pass only if she also hides the career benefit
items.explanation: If saying the motive out loud changes nothing, the mechanism does not rely on concealment. Stating a self-interested goal is not the failure.

Reciprocity, helping people consistently
Alliance-building
items.explanation: Reciprocity is helping people consistently without an immediate ask.

items.prompt: What does visibility mean in this unit?
choices: Making your job title more prominent to others
Working longer hours than the people around you
Making real work legible
items.explanation: Visibility is about sharing real work so others can see it.

items.prompt: Investing in a relationship before you need support is called what?
choices: Alliance-building
Visibility
Cold introductions
items.explanation: Alliance-building is investing early, before any specific ask.

items.prompt: Good work that nobody outside your team hears about builds what?
choices: Influence everywhere
Skill, but little influence beyond the team
Nothing at all
items.explanation: Skill grows, but influence beyond your circle needs the work to be seen.

items.prompt: An ask is best described as what?
choices: A routine status update
A compliment given to a colleague
A concrete request for support
items.explanation: An ask is a specific request, like 'please back this proposal'.

items.prompt: What is a proposal?
choices: An idea needing approval
A finished project handed to the team
A formal review of someone's performance
items.explanation: Proposals are ideas that need others to approve or back them.

items.prompt: Who are backers?
choices: People who wrote it
People willing to defend or recommend it
Budget approvers
items.explanation: Backers speak up for the proposal, often unprompted.

items.prompt: What do the three mechanisms share?
choices: Genuine investment with no immediate payoff
A hidden agenda
Fast results within the first week or two of effort
items.explanation: All three are slow, genuine, and not tied to an instant return.

items.prompt: A developer writes up a hard performance investigation and shares it with three other teams, noting what failed along the way. Which mechanism is mainly at work?
choices: Reciprocity, because she gave something away
Visibility, because real work is made legible beyond her team
Alliance-building, because three teams were involved in the sharing
None, because sharing is not politics at all
items.explanation: She is making work that already happened visible to people who would not otherwise see it. That is the visibility mechanism.
items.reference:
Three mechanisms, three surfaces
🤝 Reciprocity: acts of help, one person at a time
🔦 Visibility: real work, made legible
🧱 Alliance-building: relationships before any ask
Why: each mechanism builds trust on a different surface, and all three share genuine investment with no immediate payoff.
items.learnMore:
One pattern, three surfaces

Reciprocity covers individual acts, visibility covers work that already happened, and alliance-building covers ongoing relationships. They reinforce each other rather than compete.

Common mistake

Treating them as three unrelated tricks instead of one pattern applied in three places.
items.reflection: Which of the three mechanisms do you already use without naming it, and which would feel least natural to start?

items.prompt: A teammate keeps showing up on time and covering a director's urgent priorities for months, never asking for anything. Which description fits best?
choices: Visibility, since the director sees the effort
Transactional trading, since a payoff is hoped for
Reciprocity only, since a director is involved
Alliance-building, since the investment comes before any ask is made
items.explanation: Reliable investment in a person whose future support may matter, with no ask yet, is alliance-building.

A hidden obligation that grows over time
One transaction, no lasting trust
items.explanation: An explicit swap settles the exchange and builds nothing lasting.

Goodwill the person repays on their own initiative
Suspicion about your motives
items.explanation: Unprompted repayment is the mark of the accumulated-goodwill pattern.

Extra generous
Neutral and quickly forgotten by everyone involved
items.explanation: Calling it in recolors the help as having been a setup.

items.prompt: Does telling someone 'I help you because I value working with you' break genuine reciprocity?
choices: Yes, it ruins the goodwill that was building
No, it works the same
Yes, unless you say it only in private
items.explanation: Genuine reciprocity does not depend on being unnoticed.

items.prompt: In the model, how does the reading change as the gap grows?
choices: It rises with more months
It drops
It stays flat until the final month, then jumps
items.explanation: More time between help and ask makes the ask read as more genuine.

items.prompt: In the model, how many months is the cap?
choices: At 6 months
At 24 months
At the 12-month cap
items.explanation: The model stops adding at 12 months.

items.prompt: What does the middle pattern require most?
items.explanation: The payoff is neither immediate nor guaranteed.

items.prompt: A same-month ask in the model reads about how genuine?
choices: Patience and genuine investment
A written agreement
Quick, visible payback within days
items.explanation: Zero months of daylight gives the 15% base.

items.prompt: In the unit's model, Maya asks four months after her last unprompted help and Lena asks eight months after hers. What is the difference?
choices: Lena's ask reads 50 points more, 80% against 30%
Lena's reads twice as genuine, 80% against 40%
They read the same, because both passed month three
Lena's ask reads 25 points more genuine, 65% against 40%
items.explanation: 15 + 6.25 x 4 = 40 and 15 + 6.25 x 8 = 65, a gap of 25 points. The others use numbers the model does not produce.
items.reference:
Three ways help can be given
🔁 Explicit swap: settles one deal, no trust
🌱 Consistent, no immediate ask: goodwill builds
📣 Called in right after: recolored as transactional
Why: the middle pattern works because repayment arrives on the other person's own initiative, not because you named the debt.
items.learnMore:
The timing of an ask changes the meaning of earlier help

The same help can read as generosity or as setup, depending on how much daylight sits before the ask. This unit's model: a 15% base reading, plus 6.25 points per month, capped at 12 months.

Common mistake

Believing that honest help is automatically safe from reading as transactional.

choices: Yes, bigger is better
No, it means sharing accurate work
Only for big results
items.explanation: Visibility is accuracy made legible, not inflation.

items.prompt: What is a postmortem?
choices: A write-up of what was learned
A meeting held mainly to assign blame afterward
A formal review of one person's performance
items.explanation: Postmortems explain what happened, why, and what was learned.

items.prompt: What is a share-out?
choices: A private message
A bonus split among every member of a team after a launch
A short explanation for people who were not there
items.explanation: Share-outs bring outsiders up to speed.

items.prompt: What is a trade-off?
choices: A fair swap of favors
A choice that gains one thing and gives up another
A type of promotion
items.explanation: Trade-offs always cost something in exchange for a gain.

Very little skill, since nobody saw it
Skill, but no wider influence

items.prompt: Which is visibility rather than bragging?
choices: Explaining what a project involved
Claiming credit for the whole team's result
Hinting that you did more than the others
items.explanation: The first is accurate; the others distort.

items.prompt: Why avoid exaggeration?
choices: It takes too long
It works only while the audience believes it
It is rarely noticed
items.explanation: Exaggeration depends on people not knowing the truth.

items.prompt: Who benefits when you share a useful postmortem?
choices: Only you
Only the manager who reads it first, before anyone else
People who can avoid the same problem
items.explanation: Others learn, which is why sharing is useful and not just self-promotion.

items.prompt: Two write-ups. One gives an accurate account of a hard trade-off and what was lost. The other implies sole credit for a team result. Which passes the transparency test?
choices: The second, because it shows more impact and gets noticed faster
Both, because both were shared publicly with the wider team
The first; it survives full disclosure
Neither, because sharing work is always a kind of self-promotion
items.explanation: An accurate account survives readers knowing everything. The inflated one works only while they do not.
items.reference:
Visible versus hidden good work
🛠️ Good work, never shared: skill only
🔦 Shared deliberately: skill plus wider trust
🚫 Exaggerated: fails, it needs the audience to be fooled
Why: sharing accurate work makes true information available; inflating it needs the audience not to know.
items.learnMore:
Legible work builds trust beyond your circle

A postmortem, a share-out, or a clear account of a trade-off lets people who never worked with you judge your judgment. Accuracy is what keeps it legitimate.

Common mistake

Avoiding sharing because it feels boastful, which leaves good work unseen.
items.reflection: Think of a piece of work you are proud of. Who outside your immediate circle has actually seen it?

items.explanation: Influence needs an audience. Work that is never made legible gives outsiders nothing to base trust on.

items.prompt: What is alliance-building?

Forming a group to oppose a rival team
Asking powerful people for favors early
items.explanation: It is early, patient relationship investment.

items.prompt: What is a cold introduction?

A first real contact made only when you need something
A formal HR meeting

Someone who writes most of the code for the proposal

After the proposal has already been approved
Well before any ask

items.prompt: Which action is alliance-building?

Helping with someone's priorities, no ask
Asking for a favor in the same breath as the help
items.explanation: Early help without a request builds the base.

items.prompt: Is alliance-building a one-time push?

Their trust helps others trust you

Spend months helping with the executive's priorities, then ask

items.explanation: Backing lands on trust that already exists. A cold ask meets a stranger.

Cold introduction versus an established base

⏳ Sustained, not a one-time push
Why: an ask lands on whatever relationship already exists, so build it before the need.

A sponsor lends some of their credibility to a proposal, but only if a relationship exists. Alliance-building is the ongoing habit that creates it.

Common mistake

Treating networking as a push you do right before a request.
items.reflection: Who might you need support from in the next year? What have you done for them in the past six months with no request attached?

items.prompt: Why can a sponsor's backing not be built in the week you need it?
choices: Sponsors only meet people on Fridays
They have no time for any request
Their willingness to lend credibility rests on trust built earlier
Their backing is bought with favors that must be repaid in the very same week
items.explanation: Credibility is lent only to people the sponsor already trusts, and trust takes time.
items.reference:
Cold introduction versus an established base
🥶 Meet only when you need something: cold
🔥 Invest before any ask: trust already exists
⏳ Sustained, not a one-time push
Why: an ask lands on whatever relationship already exists, so build it before the need.

items.prompt: How many unprompted backers did A have?
choices: One
Seven
Three, each offering independently
items.explanation: Three people offered independently.

items.prompt: How long did A spend helping before the proposal?
choices: About a week, just before the ask
About three years of steady effort
About a year
items.explanation: A's investment ran roughly a year.

items.prompt: What did A do in months 4 to 6?
choices: Shared a postmortem and a share-out
Drafted the proposal
Asked three colleagues for support in advance
items.explanation: Those months were visibility.

items.prompt: What did A do in months 7 to 9?
choices: Asked for a promotion
Helped a colleague prepare a high-stakes presentation
Switched teams
items.explanation: That help was for a nearby team.

items.prompt: Was A's help attached to an ask?
choices: No, none of it was
Yes, every act
Yes, but only in the final month
items.explanation: None of A's help came with a request.

items.prompt: What is a production issue?
choices: A practice exercise run in a training environment
A budget disagreement between two different teams
A real problem on the live service
items.explanation: It affects the live service.

items.prompt: What is a PR in this scenario?
choices: A press release
A proposed code change that someone else reviews
A public relations team
items.explanation: A PR is a change submitted for review.

items.prompt: Why did each backer have their own reason to help?
choices: A asked them to
They had all been assigned by management
Each had seen A's help or judgment
items.explanation: Each backer's trust came from a separate experience.

items.prompt: Which of A's three backers most clearly came from the visibility mechanism?
choices: The colleague A helped debug on a Friday
The nearby-team colleague who received help preparing a presentation
None, since visibility builds no backers at all
The person who read the postmortem and trusted A's judgment
items.explanation: The postmortem made A's judgment visible to someone outside the team, which is the visibility mechanism.

🐛 Friday debugging help: reciprocity
📝 Shared postmortem: visibility
🎤 Presentation prep for a nearby team: alliance-building
Why: each backer came from a different act, none aimed at the proposal when it happened.
items.learnMore:
A year of habits, not a campaign

A's actions were useful at the time and each created a separate source of trust. The proposal in months 10 to 12 simply met that trust.

Common mistake

Reading A's year as a hidden plan, when each act stood on its own.
items.reflection: Look at the last year of your own work. Which of your acts could one day become a reason someone backs you?

They secretly set up a future request

They were required before drafting any proposal
items.explanation: Unconnected help is what keeps it reading as help. It still creates a backer later.

items.prompt: Did Engineer B say anything untrue?
choices: No, B was honest
Yes, in several of the coffee chats
Yes, but only in the final month
items.explanation: B's problem was timing, not honesty.

items.prompt: What did B's outreach look like to others?
choices: A kind gift
Networking with an agenda
A formal complaint
items.explanation: The compressed timing signaled an agenda.

items.prompt: In which month did B start outreach?
choices: Month 1
Month 12
Month 10
items.explanation: B waited until a proposal was coming.

items.prompt: What did B do in months 1 to 9?
choices: Solid work within one team
Wide networking across the whole company
Almost nothing at all for nine months
items.explanation: B did not build cross-team relationships.

items.prompt: What modeled genuineness did A's 12 months give?
items.explanation: At the 12-month cap the model reads 90%.

items.prompt: What modeled genuineness did B's 1 month give?
choices: About 21%, just above the 15% base
About 90%
About 50%
items.explanation: One month gives 15 plus 6.25, rounded to 21.

items.prompt: What matters more for reading outreach?
choices: A single sentence taken alone
The tone of the opening hello
The overall pattern
items.explanation: People judge the pattern, not each line.

items.prompt: How many people offered unprompted support to B?
choices: Three
None who actively did
More than for A, thanks to B's coffee chats
items.explanation: The reception was polite but lukewarm.

items.prompt: Every one of B's chats was honest. What most explains the agenda reading?
choices: The people B met simply did not like B personally
Honest statements cannot build any trust at all
Compression into the month before the ask
B scheduled too many coffee meetings in a single week
items.explanation: The pattern, not any single statement, signaled preparation for a request.
items.reference:
Same honesty, different pattern
✅ Both: no dishonest statements
📅 A: about 12 months before the ask, modeled 90%
📅 B: 1 month, modeled 21%
Why: legitimacy is judged across the whole pattern in time, not conversation by conversation.
items.learnMore:
Pattern is what the audience reads

People rarely audit individual sentences. They notice whether help arrived on its own or just ahead of a request, and they judge the entire relationship from that.

Common mistake

Checking each conversation for honesty and concluding the whole pattern must be fine.
items.reflection: Think of an outreach you received just before someone's request. What about its timing, rather than its content, shaped your reaction?

75 points, 90% against 15%
11 points, 90% against 79%
items.explanation: A reads 90% and B reads 15 + 6.25, which rounds to 21%, so the gap is 69 points.

items.prompt: Does white influence guarantee your proposal is adopted?
choices: No, it only improves the odds of a fair hearing
Yes, always
Yes, after a year
items.explanation: It cannot rescue a bad idea.

items.prompt: Can influence be genuine and strategic at once?
choices: No, any strategy ruins the sincerity of it
Yes, both can be true
Only if you are the manager of the team
items.explanation: The test is about concealment, not awareness.

items.prompt: Is sharing real work accurately self-promotion?
choices: No, it makes true information available
Yes, always
Only if you share it more than twice a year
items.explanation: Accurate sharing is not boasting.

items.prompt: What is the main mistake of starting only when you need it?
choices: It costs too much
Nobody has time
The compressed timing makes the pattern look transactional
items.explanation: Compressed investment reads as setup.

items.prompt: Was A as calculating as B?
choices: Yes, only better hidden
Yes, but A simply started earlier in the year
No, A's pattern passes the test
items.explanation: Pattern and timing differ, not self-awareness.

items.prompt: What if the proposal is wrong?
choices: Influence will not fix it
Backers will quietly hide the flaws for you
Trust alone will carry it through approval
items.explanation: Trust gets a hearing, not a pass.

items.prompt: Who might misread visibility as boasting?
choices: A new manager
Someone uncomfortable with sharing their work
No one
items.explanation: Discomfort is the usual cause.

items.prompt: Is honesty alone enough?
choices: No, the pattern in time matters too
Yes, completely
Only if everything is also put in writing first
items.explanation: Both A and B were honest.

items.prompt: A says, 'I did understand that my helping builds trust.' Which verdict is correct?
choices: It proves A was as calculating as B
Understanding the benefit does not disqualify it, since nothing depends on concealment
It means A must stop helping
It means A's help was fake all along
items.explanation: The test asks whether the mechanism needs the other person not to understand. Awareness of the benefit is not concealment.
items.reference:
Where the model stops
🎲 Improves odds, does not guarantee adoption
🧠 Genuine and strategic can coexist
🔦 Skipping visibility leaves work unseen
⏱️ Starting only when you need it is too late
Why: the method makes a fair hearing more likely; it cannot rescue a bad proposal or substitute for time.
items.learnMore:
Four ways to misread the case

Starting late, avoiding visibility, confusing genuine with unstrategic, and expecting guarantees are the main misreadings. Each comes from treating the model as a formula.

Common mistake

Treating legitimate influence as a formula that guarantees the outcome.
items.reflection: Which of the four failure modes are you most likely to fall into, and what would you change to avoid it?

items.prompt: A's proposal got three unprompted backers. What can honestly be concluded?

The proposal must be correct
The backers will approve it regardless of any flaws it carries later
The odds of a fair hearing improved, with no guarantee
items.explanation: Support is a plausible outcome of the pattern, not a certainty. A flawed proposal can still fail.
